opus-5.5.text:
That's a very real concern, and it's something we think about a lot. When you train a single model on both language and visual data, you're asking it to serve two different masters. Language is very compact and abstract. A sentence like "the cup falls off the table" carries a lot of meaning in a few tokens. Video is the opposite: it's extremely high-dimensional, and most of the information is low-level detail about geometry, lighting, motion, contact. So there's a legitimate worry that if you optimize for one, you degrade the other. You've probably seen this in vision-language models, where adding a lot of visual training can hurt the language reasoning, or the model learns to lean on language priors and stops really looking at the pixels.

The way I think about it is that, for physical AI, the two signals play different roles, and you should design the system so they complement each other instead of competing. Language is very good for specifying intent, the task, and high-level reasoning: what should happen, and why. Vision, especially video, is where you learn physics: how objects move, how they deform, what happens when a robot arm pushes something. You can't learn that from text alone, because nobody writes down every detail of how a towel folds. So the visual model has to carry the burden of understanding the physical world, and language should condition it and help it reason, not replace it.

In practice, that means a few things. One is data balance and curation. You need a huge amount of high-quality video showing real physical interactions, not just text-heavy data with images attached. Another is architecture: how you tokenize the visual signal, and how you let language attend to it, matters a lot. If the visual tokens are too compressed, you lose the physics. If they're too raw, the model struggles to connect them to language. Then there's training staging. Often it works better to first build a strong world model that understands video dynamics, and then align it with language, rather than mixing everything from the start and hoping it works out.

I'd also say interference isn't purely bad. Some of that tension is the model learning to ground language in physical reality, and that's exactly what we want. The word "fragile" should mean something about how an object behaves when it's dropped. Getting there requires the two modalities to push on each other. The goal isn't to keep them separate; it's to manage the interaction so you get grounding without one modality collapsing the other.

So my short answer: the concern is valid, but I see it as an engineering and research problem we can address with the right data, tokenization, and training recipe, not a fundamental barrier. And for physical AI, I think we have to solve it, because a robot needs to understand both what you're asking and how the world will respond when it acts.

r001.rationale: It contrasts compact, abstract language with detailed video and says video teaches physical dynamics that text alone cannot capture.

r002.rationale: It says a robot needs to understand what a person is asking, making human communication a reason to understand language.

r003.rationale: It connects physical AI to robot action and says the robot needs to understand how the world responds when it acts.

r004.rationale: It discusses modality roles and managing interference, but does not state that whether interference occurs depends on the model’s intended purpose.

r005.rationale: It assigns video a central role in learning physics, but does not suggest that machines could develop intelligence directly from visual observations without adopting human language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we thought about a lot when we were designing Cosmos. And honestly, I think the concern is real, but it's a little bit misframed.

The worry usually goes like this: language is a very compressed, abstract signal. A sentence like "the robot picks up the cup" throws away almost everything about the physics — the weight of the cup, how the fingers close, how the arm compensates. Vision, on the other hand, is extremely dense. Every frame carries a huge amount of information about geometry, contact, lighting, motion. So if you mix them, people assume the language will "pull" the model toward shortcuts — it learns to predict words instead of learning the physics — or the visual stream will drown out the language and the model stops listening to instructions at all.

What we've found is that interference happens mostly when you force the two modalities to share the wrong representation. If you treat video tokens and text tokens as the same kind of thing, and just dump them into one sequence and hope for the best, yes, you get competition. The model has a fixed capacity, the gradients from the two objectives don't agree, and the dense signal usually wins.

But for physical AI, I actually think of language and vision as playing different roles rather than competing for the same role. Video is the substrate — that's where the world model lives, that's where the model learns how things move, how objects interact, what happens when you push something off a table. Language is a steering signal on top of that. It's not there to teach the model physics; it's there to specify intent, to index into the space of possible futures. "Pick up the red cup, not the blue one." The text doesn't need to know how the fingers close. It just needs to pick the branch.

Once you see it that way, the design becomes clearer. You want the visual tokenizer and the visual pretraining to be strong enough that the model already has a good physical prior before language gets very involved. Then language conditioning is relatively light-touch — cross-attention, or a conditioning pathway — so it modulates the generation rather than rewriting it. In our experience, when the visual foundation is strong, adding language doesn't degrade the physics. If anything it helps, because a lot of the ambiguity in video — what is this person about to do? — is resolved by the caption.

The place where I'd say the concern is really valid is data quality. If your captions are bad, or if they describe things that aren't actually in the video, then you are teaching the model that language and vision are only loosely correlated, and the model learns to ignore one of them. So a surprising amount of the work isn't architecture at all. It's building captioning pipelines that are actually grounded, that describe motion and physical interaction, not just "a kitchen with a man in it."

And then the last thing I'd say — for physical AI, language isn't even the only conditioning signal. You have actions, you have camera poses, you have proprioception from the robot. Language is one of several. So I'd rather build a system where the visual world model is the common core and everything else is a way to condition it, than a system where language and vision are somehow equal partners fighting over the same parameters. That framing has made the interference problem much less scary for us in practice.

r002.rationale: It says language can specify intent and instructions, but does not identify communication with humans as a reason the model needs language.

r003.rationale: It discusses learning how objects move and interact, but does not state that understanding action is necessary for physical AI to change the world.

r004.rationale: It says interference arises when modalities are forced into the wrong shared representation, then frames their roles for physical AI as a visual world model conditioned by language and other signals.

r005.rationale: It describes a strong visual foundation with language as conditioning, but does not suggest machines could develop intelligence directly from visual observations without adopting human language’s framework.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real concern, but combining language and vision doesn’t necessarily mean they will interfere. They can also complement each other. Language helps express intent and abstract concepts, while vision provides information about the physical world. The question is how we train the model to use each signal appropriately.

For example, if the instruction is to pick up a cup, language tells you the goal. But it doesn’t tell you exactly where the cup is or how its position changes as you move. Those decisions need to be grounded in visual observations. You don’t want a strong language prior to override what the system actually sees.

So I would treat interference as something to measure. Does adding language improve task understanding while preserving spatial accuracy? Can the model respond correctly when the observation contradicts what it would normally expect? For physical AI, success has to be judged by what the system can reliably do in the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vision grounding decisions in visual observations, but does not say video represents physical operations more precisely than language.

r002.rationale: It does not identify communication with humans as a reason a physical AI model needs to understand language.

r003.rationale: It discusses acting on a task, but does not state that understanding action is necessary for physical AI to change the world.

r004.rationale: It recommends measuring effects on task understanding and spatial accuracy, but does not say whether a modality is interference depends on the model’s intended purpose.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that machines could develop intelligence directly from visual observations without human language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a valid concern. Language and vision carry different kinds of information, and if you combine them carelessly, one can dominate the other. Language gives you a useful abstraction of the world, but for physical AI, that abstraction is not enough. Knowing that an object is a cup doesn’t tell you its exact geometry, where to grasp it, or how it will move when you touch it.

So I would distinguish combining information from forcing everything into the same representation. You want language to help communicate intent and provide semantic context, while preserving the spatial and temporal information in the visual signal that matters for action.

Whether those signals help or interfere is ultimately an empirical question. Does adding language improve the system’s ability to predict what happens next and choose the right action? Can it still respond to visual details that weren’t described in words? For physical AI, that grounding in the world has to remain central.
